title: Urine Concentration and Timed Collections: Isosthenuria, ACR and the Full Jug
summary: Learn what a fixed specific gravity of 1.010 means, why the first-morning sample is preferred for chemistry, how to judge a 24-hour collection by its creatinine, why albuminuria is reported as an albumin-to-creatinine ratio, and why volume cutoffs describe rather than diagnose.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 29 Hits 3, 10, 11 and 19 and Trap 6. Checked against Simerville 2005 (AAFP page), Caleffi 2010 (journal page), Sacks 2011, McGill 2022, Chagnac 2024, Forni Ogna 2015, Newell-Price 2025 and Klein 2018. The StatPearls “Urinalysis” chapter (NCBI Bookshelf) was blocked by a captcha page and was not read. Sacks 2023 (Diabetes Care) could not be re-read at fact-check (PMC captcha, publisher 403, Europe PMC full text not available), so it is not cited. Where the sources qualify the reviewer the lesson teaches the source: 24-hour creatinine 20–25 mg/kg/day is the male range (women 15–20) and dated; polyuria is taught as ≥ 3 L/24 h or > 40–50 mL/kg/24 h rather than > 2.5 L/day; oliguria as < 0.5 mL/kg/h over 6 h; second-morning urine may be better for cell morphology; albuminuria categories use the ACR or timed excretion, not a 30–300 mg/L concentration window. Not taught (not found in the sources read): oliguria < 400 mL/day, anuria < 100 mL/day, “earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy”, “dead kidneys”.

objectives: Explain isosthenuria as a specific gravity fixed at 1.010 on repeated samples.
Choose first-morning, second-morning or midstream urine for chemistry, cell morphology and culture.
Judge a 24-hour collection with sex-specific creatinine excretion and report albuminuria as an albumin-to-creatinine ratio.
Interpret polyuria and oliguria cutoffs with urine osmolality and the clinical picture.

scenes.title: Three urine numbers, one bench
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: three urine results on one bench. (1) A 24-hour jug from a 70-kg man containing 800 mg of creatinine, sent for a protein excretion study. (2) A random afternoon urine from a patient with type 2 diabetes: albumin 45 mg/L, no creatinine measured. (3) A patient whose urine specific gravity reads 1.010 on every sample over several days, with 3.2 L of urine in 24 hours. Question token: “Which number can you trust on its own?”

cues.text: Three urine numbers arrive. A 24-hour jug from a 70-kilogram man holding 800 milligrams of creatinine. A random afternoon urine from a diabetic patient: albumin 45 milligrams per litre.
And a patient whose specific gravity reads 1.010 on every sample, with 3.2 litres of urine in a day.
Which of these numbers can you trust on its own?

props.label: Which number can you trust on its own?

scenes.title: A healthy kidney concentrates on demand
scenes.altText: Schematic: a specific gravity scale from 1.003 to 1.030. Below 1.010 = relative hydration; above 1.020 = relative dehydration (Simerville 2005). Specimen card: the first-morning void, collected after about 8 hours lying down and at least 4 hours in the bladder, is often preferred for chemical analysis; for detailed cell morphology (glomerular vs non-glomerular haematuria, atypical cells, decoy cells) a second-morning void may be preferable because long bladder dwell can damage cells (Caleffi 2010). Midstream card: discard the first part of the stream; midstream urine suits culture and is also the most suitable for physical, chemical and morphological analysis because it carries the least urethral contamination.

cues.text: A healthy kidney changes urine concentration on demand. Specific gravity can range from about 1.003 to 1.030. Below 1.010 suggests relative hydration; above 1.020, relative dehydration.
The first-morning void, after about eight hours lying down and at least four hours in the bladder, is often preferred for chemical analysis.
But long bladder time can damage cells. For detailed cell morphology, such as dysmorphic red cells or atypical cells, a second-morning void may be better.
Whatever the time of day, collect midstream: discard the first part of the stream. Midstream urine suits culture and the routine physical, chemical and microscopic examination.

scenes.title: When concentration and volume go wrong
scenes.altText: Isosthenuria card: in intrinsic renal insufficiency, specific gravity becomes fixed at 1.010, the specific gravity of the glomerular filtrate — the tubules no longer dilute or concentrate (Simerville 2005). A single 1.010 lies inside the normal range; “fixed” means the same value on repeated samples. Polyuria card (Newell-Price 2025): least stringent criteria are ≥3 L/24 h in adults (≥2 L/m²/24 h in children) or >40 mL/kg/24 h; some studies use >50 mL/kg/24 h. The next step is urine osmolality: ≤300 mOsm/kg = hypotonic (water) diuresis; ≥800 mOsm/kg = solute diuresis (glucose, sodium, urea, mannitol). Primary polydipsia also produces polyuria. Oliguria card (Klein 2018): most commonly <0.5 mL/kg/h over 6 h (definitions vary); it can be physiological (hypovolaemia, fasting, after ultra-endurance events) or pathological (acute kidney injury).

cues.text: In intrinsic renal disease the tubules stop diluting and concentrating. Specific gravity becomes fixed at 1.010, the specific gravity of the glomerular filtrate. That is isosthenuria.
One reading of 1.010 is inside the normal range. Fixed means the same value on repeated samples.

Volume needs the same care. Polyuria has no single agreed definition; three litres or more in twenty-four hours in adults, or more than forty to fifty millilitres per kilogram, is used. Urine osmolality comes next: three hundred or less is hypotonic; eight hundred or more means solute diuresis, such as glucose.

Oliguria is most often defined as less than half a millilitre per kilogram per hour over six hours. It can be a normal response to fluid loss or fasting, or a sign of acute kidney injury. The cutoff describes volume, not cause.

scenes.title: Give every number a denominator
scenes.altText: Completeness card (Forni Ogna 2015): traditional 24-hour creatinine excretion references are 20–25 mg/kg/day for men and 15–20 mg/kg/day for women; they date from the 1960s–1970s and would flag more than half of collections in a Swiss population (two-thirds over age 60) as inaccurate, so age- and BMI-based references have been proposed. Worked example: 800 mg ÷ 70 kg ≈ 11.4 mg/kg/day, far below the male range: under-collected. Albuminuria card (McGill 2022; Sacks 2011; Chagnac 2024): albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR) categories A1 <30 mg/g, A2 30–300 mg/g (moderately increased; Sacks 2011 notes the band was formerly called microalbuminuria), A3 >300 mg/g; timed equivalents 30–300 mg/24 h or 20–200 µg/min; the ratio corrects for urine concentration and dilution; a first-morning void is preferable for the ratio; confirm on 2 of 3 tests over 3–6 months; chemical strips are not sensitive at 20–50 mg/L. Hook answers card.

cues.text: A 24-hour result is only as good as the jug. Creatinine output checks it: the traditional reference is 20 to 25 milligrams per kilogram per day in men and 15 to 20 in women. Our man: 800 divided by 70 is about 11 milligrams per kilogram. The jug is probably under-collected.
These ranges are old and do not allow for age or body size; in one large study they would have flagged over half of all collections, so newer references adjust for both.

Albumin needs a denominator too. The albumin-to-creatinine ratio corrects for how dilute the urine is. Thirty to three hundred milligrams per gram is moderately increased albuminuria, once called microalbuminuria. Use a first-morning sample and confirm on two of three tests.
Hook answers: the jug is probably under-collected; 45 milligrams per litre cannot be categorised without creatinine; and a fixed 1.010 with 3.2 litres needs osmolality and the clinical picture.

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “One SG of 1.010 = isosthenuria” (✓ isosthenuria means fixed at 1.010 on repeated samples; one 1.010 is in the normal range); “Albumin 45 mg/L = moderately increased albuminuria” (✓ categories use the ACR or a timed excretion rate; a concentration does not correct for dilution); “Expect 20–25 mg/kg/day of creatinine from everyone” (✓ that is the traditional male range; women 15–20 mg/kg/day, and age and body size matter).

cues.text: Trap one: a single specific gravity of 1.010 means isosthenuria. No: isosthenuria is a fixed value on repeated samples.
Trap two: albumin of 45 milligrams per litre is moderately increased albuminuria. No: categories use the ratio to creatinine or a timed excretion rate.
Trap three: expect 20 to 25 milligrams per kilogram of creatinine from everyone. No: that is the traditional male range; women run lower, and age and body size matter.

scenes.title: Fixed, Full, Fraction
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Fixed, Full, Fraction.” FIXED: specific gravity stuck at 1.010 on repeat = isosthenuria. FULL: creatinine per kilogram proves the 24-hour jug is full. FRACTION: albumin over creatinine (ACR) corrects for dilution. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: Fixed, Full, Fraction. Fixed: specific gravity stuck at 1.010 on repeat is isosthenuria. Full: creatinine per kilogram proves the jug is full. Fraction: albumin over creatinine corrects for dilution.

Where it breaks: creatinine output depends on sex, age and muscle mass, so a low value is not always a missed void; the ratio still varies from day to day, so it needs repeat tests; and volume cutoffs differ between definitions.

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “24-h jug → creatinine per kg · albumin → ACR on a first-morning void”, “Isosthenuria = SG fixed at 1.010 on repeat · volume cutoffs describe, osmolality explains”.

cues.text: Read every urine number against its denominator: check a 24-hour jug with its creatinine output, report albuminuria as an albumin-to-creatinine ratio on a first-morning sample, and call isosthenuria only when specific gravity stays fixed on repeated samples.

props.label: Isosthenuria = SG fixed at 1.010 on repeat samples

explanation.what: Plain language: a urine number means little until you know how concentrated the urine was and whether the whole sample was collected. Healthy kidneys swing urine from dilute to concentrated; failing tubules leave it stuck at the density of filtered plasma. Creatinine tells you whether a 24-hour jug is complete, and dividing albumin by creatinine cancels out dilution. Scientific terms: specific gravity (SG), isosthenuria, first-morning and second-morning void, midstream specimen, creatinine excretion (mg/kg/day), albumin-to-creatinine ratio (ACR), albuminuria categories A1–A3, albumin excretion rate, polyuria, oliguria, urine osmolality, water diuresis, solute diuresis.
explanation.why: Urine concentration follows hydration, so a single concentration (mg/L) reflects water balance as well as disease. Creatinine is produced at a fairly constant rate that depends on muscle mass, so its daily excretion serves as a completeness check for timed collections and as the denominator that corrects spot results for dilution.
explanation.measure: SG range about 1.003–1.030; < 1.010 relative hydration, > 1.020 relative dehydration; fixed at 1.010 in intrinsic renal insufficiency. First-morning void (~8 h recumbent, ≥ 4 h bladder dwell) preferred for chemistry and for ACR; second-morning void may be better for cell morphology. 24-h creatinine reference 20–25 mg/kg/day men, 15–20 mg/kg/day women (traditional, age- and body-size-blind). ACR A1 < 30 mg/g, A2 30–300 mg/g, A3 > 300 mg/g (timed: 30–300 mg/24 h, 20–200 µg/min); confirm on 2 of 3 tests over 3–6 months. Polyuria ≥ 3 L/24 h or > 40–50 mL/kg/24 h (adults); urine osmolality ≤ 300 mOsm/kg hypotonic, ≥ 800 solute diuresis; no universally accepted polyuria definition. Oliguria commonly < 0.5 mL/kg/h over 6 h.
explanation.differs: Single SG 1.010 (normal range) vs SG fixed at 1.010 (isosthenuria); albumin concentration (mg/L, dilution-dependent) vs ACR (mg/g, dilution-corrected); first-morning (chemistry) vs second-morning (cell morphology); physiological vs pathological oliguria; water vs solute diuresis.
explanation.examAngle: Expect: judge a 24-hour collection from its creatinine, pick the best specimen for albuminuria screening, recognise isosthenuria, or choose the next test (osmolality) after a large urine volume.

mnemonic.text: Fixed, Full, Fraction: FIXED specific gravity at 1.010 on repeat = isosthenuria; creatinine per kilogram proves the jug is FULL; albumin as a FRACTION of creatinine (ACR) corrects for dilution.
mnemonic.explanation: Three checks that turn a raw urine number into one you can interpret.
mnemonic.limitation: Creatinine output varies with sex, age and muscle mass, so a low value is not always a missed void; the ACR still varies day to day and needs repeat tests; volume cutoffs differ between definitions and do not give a cause.

analogyLimitations: Cards and the specific gravity scale are schematic.
The 24-hour creatinine ranges are traditional references; age- and body-size-based references have been proposed.
takeaway: Read every urine number against its denominator: check a 24-hour jug with its creatinine output, report albuminuria as an albumin-to-creatinine ratio on a first-morning sample, and call isosthenuria only when specific gravity stays fixed on repeated samples.

questions.stem: A 60-kg woman’s 24-hour urine collection contains 420 mg of creatinine. Using the traditional reference range for women, how should the collection be judged?

options.rationale: Correct. 420 ÷ 60 = 7 mg/kg/day, well below the traditional female reference of 15–20 mg/kg/day, so incomplete collection is likely.

options.text: Complete, because 420 mg is within 20–25 mg/kg/day
options.rationale: Incorrect. 420 mg is a total, not a per-kilogram value; 7 mg/kg/day is below both the male and female ranges.

options.text: Over-collected, because women excrete less creatinine
options.rationale: Incorrect. Lower expected output in women does not make 7 mg/kg/day high; it is low.

options.text: Cannot be judged without the urine volume
options.rationale: Incorrect. Total creatinine per kilogram of body weight is the completeness check; volume alone does not prove completeness.

questions.stem: Which specimen and result format are recommended for assessing albuminuria in a patient with diabetes?

options.text: A first-morning void reported as an albumin-to-creatinine ratio
options.rationale: Correct. The ratio corrects for urine dilution, and a first-morning void has lower within-person variation.

options.text: A random afternoon void reported as albumin in mg/L
options.rationale: Incorrect. A concentration does not correct for dilution and is not used to assign albuminuria categories.
Incorrect. Conventional strips do not detect the small increases of albumin that define moderately increased albuminuria.

options.text: A single test, without repeats, to make the diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. Increased albumin excretion should be shown on two of three tests over 3–6 months.

questions.stem: Over several days a patient’s urine specific gravity reads 1.010 on every sample. What does this pattern most likely indicate?

options.text: Isosthenuria: loss of tubular diluting and concentrating ability
options.rationale: Correct. A specific gravity fixed at 1.010, that of the glomerular filtrate, is the pattern of intrinsic renal insufficiency.

options.text: Normal kidneys, because 1.010 is in the reference range
options.rationale: Incorrect. One 1.010 can be normal; the same value on every sample shows the kidney is not responding to changing intake.
Incorrect. Dehydrated healthy kidneys produce a high specific gravity, above about 1.020.
Incorrect. Healthy kidneys dilute urine below 1.010 after a water load.

Urine specific gravity can range from 1.003 to 1.030; < 1.010 relative hydration, > 1.020 relative dehydration; in intrinsic renal insufficiency SG is fixed at 1.010, the specific gravity of the glomerular filtrate. references.citation: Caleffi A, Manoni F, Alessio MG, Ottomano C, Lippi G. Quality in the extra-analytical phases of urinalysis. Biochem Med (Zagreb). 2010;20(2):179-183. doi:10.11613/BM.2010.022
references.usedFor: First-void morning urine may be preferred for chemical analysis; early-morning urine after 8 h recumbence and ≥ 4 h bladder storage; second-void specimen may be preferable for cell type and morphology (glomerular vs non-glomerular haematuria, atypical cells, decoy cells) because bladder dwell can compromise cell shape and integrity; discard the first part of the stream; midstream urine suitable for physical, chemical and morphological analysis (minimal urethral contamination).

references.citation: Sacks DB, Arnold M, Bakris GL, et al. Guidelines and recommendations for laboratory analysis in the diagnosis and management of diabetes mellitus. Diabetes Care. 2011;34(6):e61-e99. doi:10.2337/dc11-9998
references.usedFor: Albuminuria section: Table 8 definitions (30–300 mg/24 h, 20–200 µg/min, 30–300 µg/mg creatinine; formerly microalbuminuria), two of three collections; conventional dipsticks do not detect small increases and are insensitive at 20–50 mg/L; first-morning void preferable for the ratio (lower within-person variation); untimed albumin concentration only for screening with a high-sensitivity cutoff; 24-h collections often inadequate and creatinine not routinely checked; transient increases with exercise, infection, fever, hyperglycaemia; low-level albuminuria alone indicates neither kidney disease per se nor progression risk without hypertension.

references.citation: McGill JB, Haller H, Roy-Chaudhury P, Cherrington A, Wada T, Wanner C, Ji L, Rossing P. Making an impact on kidney disease in people with type 2 diabetes: the importance of screening for albuminuria. BMJ Open Diabetes Res Care. 2022;10(4):e002806. doi:10.1136/bmjdrc-2022-002806
references.usedFor: Albuminuria categories in CKD: A1 (normal to mildly increased) UACR < 30 mg/g, A2 (moderately increased) 30–300 mg/g, A3 (severely increased) > 300 mg/g; UACR measured on spot urine, preferably the first morning void; dipsticks have poor sensitivity for UACR ≥ 30 mg/g.

references.citation: Chagnac A, Friedman AN. Measuring Albuminuria in Individuals With Obesity: Pitfalls of the Urinary Albumin-Creatinine Ratio. Kidney Med. 2024;6(4):100804. doi:10.1016/j.xkme.2024.100804
references.usedFor: The ACR corrects for urine concentration and dilution compared with albumin concentration alone; urinary creatinine excretion mostly reflects muscle mass, is higher in men, falls with age; ACR has large (median 33%) day-to-day within-person variability.

references.citation: Forni Ogna V, Ogna A, Vuistiner P, Pruijm M, Ponte B, Ackermann D, et al. New anthropometry-based age- and sex-specific reference values for urinary 24-hour creatinine excretion based on the adult Swiss population. BMC Med. 2015;13:40. doi:10.1186/s12916-015-0275-x
references.usedFor: Urinary creatinine excretion as a completeness marker for timed collections; current reference values 20–25 mg/kg/24 h (177–221 µmol/kg) in men and 15–20 mg/kg/24 h (133–177 µmol/kg) in women, derived from 1960s–1970s observations; applying them would flag 56% of collections (67% over age 60) as inaccurate; proposed age-, sex- and BMI-based references.

references.citation: Newell-Price J, Drummond JB, Gurnell M, Levy M, McCormack A, Cooper D, et al. Approach to the Patient With Suspected Hypotonic Polyuria. J Clin Endocrinol Metab. 2025;110(2):e506-e514. doi:10.1210/clinem/dgae565
references.usedFor: Polyuria thresholds: past studies used ≥ 3 L/24 h in adults (≥ 2 L/m²/24 h in children) or > 40 or > 50 mL/kg/24 h; least stringent criteria ≥ 3 L/24 h or > 40 mL/kg/24 h; next step urine osmolality (≤ 300 mOsm/kg hypotonic; ≥ 800 mOsm/kg solute diuresis from glucose, sodium, urea or mannitol); primary polydipsia as a cause.

references.citation: Klein SJ, Lehner GF, Forni LG, Joannidis M. Oliguria in critically ill patients: a narrative review. J Nephrol. 2018;31(6):855-862. doi:10.1007/s40620-018-0539-6

claims.text: SG range about 1.003–1.030; < 1.010 relative hydration, > 1.020 relative dehydration; SG fixed at 1.010 (glomerular filtrate) in intrinsic renal insufficiency.
claims.note: That a single 1.010 lies within the normal range is inferred from the stated range. Simerville describes the fixed 1.010 pattern without the word “isosthenuria”; the label is the curriculum term and no open source read defines it.

claims.text: First-morning void preferred for chemistry; second-morning void may be better for cell morphology; midstream collection.
24-hour creatinine excretion references by sex, their age/body-size limitations, creatinine production tied to muscle mass, and the under-collection arithmetic.
Albuminuria categories (ACR, timed equivalents), dilution correction, first-morning void, two of three tests, dipstick insensitivity, day-to-day ACR variability.
Polyuria thresholds (no universally accepted definition) and urine osmolality next step; oliguria definition and physiological vs pathological causes.
Reviewer’s oliguria < 400 mL/day, anuria < 100 mL/day, polyuria > 2.5 L/day, “earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy” and a 30–300 mg/L albumin concentration window.

accuracyFlags.issue: Ch. 29 Hit 19 gives 20–25 mg/kg/day as the expected 24-hour creatinine excretion for everyone. Forni Ogna 2015 gives this as the traditional male range (women 15–20 mg/kg/day) and shows the 1960s–1970s ranges would misclassify over half of collections (two-thirds over age 60); the lesson teaches sex-specific ranges and their limits (register flag rv-creatinine-excretion-sex).

Ch. 29 Trap 6 and the Number Vault define polyuria as > 2.5 L/day. Newell-Price 2025 states there is no universally accepted definition, lists ≥ 3 L/24 h in adults or > 40–50 mL/kg/24 h as thresholds used in past studies, and calls ≥ 3 L or > 40 mL/kg the least stringent criteria; the lesson teaches these (register flag rv-polyuria-threshold).

Ch. 29 Trap 6 defines oliguria as < 400 mL/day and anuria as < 100 mL/day. Klein 2018 gives the most common definition as < 0.5 mL/kg/h over 6 h with other periods and cutoffs in use; the mL/day figures were not found in the sources read and are not taught (register flag rv-oliguria-definition).

Ch. 29 Hit 10 says the first-morning specimen is best for formed elements. Caleffi 2010 says first-morning urine may be preferred for chemistry, but a second-morning void may be preferable for cell morphology because long bladder dwell can damage cells (register flag rv-first-morning-formed-elements).

Ch. 29 Hit 11 lists an albumin concentration of 30–300 mg/L as one of three equivalent definitions and calls the finding the earliest sign of diabetic nephropathy. Sacks 2011 (Table 8) and McGill 2022 define categories by ACR, mg/24 h or µg/min only; Sacks 2011 allows an untimed albumin concentration only for screening with a cutoff chosen for high sensitivity, calls albuminuria an early risk marker, and notes that low-level albuminuria alone indicates neither kidney disease per se nor progression risk unless hypertension is present (register flag rv-albumin-concentration-window).

verification.notes: 5 factual claims checked against Simerville 2005, Caleffi 2010, Sacks 2011, McGill 2022, Chagnac 2024, Forni Ogna 2015, Newell-Price 2025 and Klein 2018; 1 pending (reviewer volume cutoffs, “earliest sign” wording and mg/L window; not taught). StatPearls “Urinalysis” was blocked by a captcha and not read; Sacks 2023 could not be re-read at fact-check and is not cited. No human expert has reviewed this lesson.
